title: Meet the Siddis: Tribal Gujaratis from Kathiawad, natural athletes of African stock

summary: Khushbu Darjada, 15, became the first Siddi athlete to win a Youth Olympics medal (judo silver); the Siddis of Gujarat, of African descent, are a PVTG of about 12,959 people.

title: When a population rule shuts women out
news: The SC said the two-child bar on panchayat office 'tended to weaken the position of women rather than empowering them'.
link: A rule neutral on paper can be unequal in effect: in a patriarchal society women have little control over family size, yet bear the disqualification. Inclusive governance means testing laws for their real effect on women, not their wording.
question: "Laws that are neutral in form can be discriminatory in effect." Illustrate with reference to women's participation in local governance.

title: Rights without rivalry
news: A petition seeks to stop recognising trans women as 'females'; the author urges debate that treats transgender persons as equal rights-bearers.
link: Equality is indivisible: one marginalised group's protection cannot be secured by excluding another. Empathy and reasoned debate, not fear, should guide how competing claims are balanced.
question: How can a public servant balance competing claims of two marginalised groups while upholding the constitutional value of equality?

title: The state at the cradle
news: The Supreme Court said laws disqualifying people with more than two children from panchayat polls have lost relevance, calling the choice to have children 'most intimate and personal'.
syllabus: Ethics and human interface; Dignity and liberty; Means and ends in public policy
link: A good end, a stable population, does not justify coercive means that punish personal choices and exclude citizens from democracy. Respecting reproductive autonomy treats citizens as ends in themselves, and the burden of such laws often falls hardest on women.
question: Can a public policy goal justify restricting deeply personal choices of citizens? Discuss with reference to population policy.

title: A dormitory, not a slogan
news: Tamil Nadu employs 40.3% of India's directly employed women factory workers, helped by an innovative dormitory model adapted from China.
syllabus: Innovation and creativity in public service; Gender justice; Empathy
link: Empathy for women's real constraints, distance and safety, led to an innovative, practical fix rather than another incentive. Innovation in public service means seeing the barrier from the citizen's side and removing it.
question: "Innovation in public service begins with empathy for the citizen's real constraints." Discuss with examples.

title: More young women adopting menstrual hygiene
where: Your Health, page 12 (Policy Matters: Pally Kundu & Reena Singh, MoHFW)
syllabus: GS2 › Health; Welfare schemes for vulnerable sections and their performance · GS1 › Role of women; Social empowerment · GS4 › Dignity and compassion
summary: NFHS-6 shows 79.2% of women aged 15–24 use hygienic menstrual protection, up from 57.6% in 2015-16, the result of a multi-pronged government strategy.
ideas: A quiet social revolution: hygienic menstrual protection among women aged 15–24 has risen by about 22 percentage points since NFHS-4, so most young women have now moved off cloth and unsafe materials.
The rise in menstrual hygiene is an underrated marker of women's empowerment and public health progress.

Dignity is part of the definition: WHO–UNICEF define menstrual hygiene as clean material, changed in privacy, safely disposed of, without embarrassment or restriction, linking it to the SDGs on health and gender equality.
Menstrual hygiene is about dignity and freedom from restriction, not just products.

Multi-pronged delivery: the Scheme for Promotion of Menstrual Hygiene under the National Health Mission combines awareness for adolescent girls, subsidised napkins through ASHAs via schools and communities, and safe disposal.
Combining awareness, access and disposal through ASHAs and schools shows convergent scheme design.
Affordability through Jan Aushadhi: Suvidha sanitary pads at ₹1 each are distributed through Jan Aushadhi Kendras nationwide.
Pricing essential hygiene products at ₹1 removes cost as a barrier for poor households.
Beyond numbers: even small gains mean lakhs of young women switching to safe methods, part of a wider shift in how young women learn, decide and are heard.
Health gains among young women reinforce their education, agency and voice.
keywords: WHO–UNICEF standard of safe, private, dignified menstrual care
India tracks menstrual hygiene management against the WHO–UNICEF benchmark.
Several schemes and institutions working together
Menstrual hygiene gains show convergence of health, education and community platforms.
Services reaching households through ASHAs and schools
ASHAs show frontline delivery is the backbone of health outcomes.
